summary: A guide for people implementing Signaling Compression (SigComp). It helps with choices such as which compression algorithm to use and how robust to be against lost or misordered packets. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: SigComp squeezes messages so they take less room. This is a how-to guide with tips on which squeezing method to pick and what to do when pieces go missing.

questions: what compression algorithms does sigcomp support
subtitle: Guidelines for implementers choosing compression algorithms and robustness features for SigComp

tldr.problem: SigComp (Signaling Compression) lets network protocols compress messages by uploading decompression bytecode into a Universal Decompressor Virtual Machine, but implementers must decide which compression algorithm to use and how to protect against lost or misordered packets.
tldr.mechanism: This guide provides working bytecode for five well-known compression algorithms (LZ77, LZSS, LZW, DEFLATE, LZJH) and mechanisms for robustness such as acknowledgements, static dictionaries, CRC checks, and shared state between message flows.
tldr.outcome: SigComp implementers have concrete examples and decision criteria to choose an algorithm based on compression ratio, memory, processing power, and code size, with optional robustness features for mission-critical protocols.

today: RFC 4464 is an Informational RFC that documents SigComp implementation practice. SigComp is used in VoIP, mobile signaling, and other bandwidth-constrained protocols where message compression is critical.

sections.title: SigComp and the Universal Decompressor Virtual Machine
sections.content:
Signaling Compression (SigComp) is a protocol framework that compresses application messages before transmission. Instead of hard-coding a single compression algorithm, SigComp sends the algorithm itself as bytecode that runs on a Universal Decompressor Virtual Machine (UDVM) at the receiving endpoint.

This approach allows different applications and networks to use different compression algorithms suited to their traffic patterns, memory constraints, and processing power. The RFC provides an informational guide for implementers choosing which algorithm to use and how to write the bytecode for it.
sections.plainLanguage: SigComp is like a traffic cop that can teach the receiving end new ways to unsqueeze messages. This guide shows five recipes for squeezing and how to write the instructions for unsqueezing.

sections.title: The UDVM Assembly Language
sections.content:
The UDVM executes bytecode written in an assembly language designed for compression decompression. The language is organized in two levels:

Lexical level: tokens like instruction opcodes, variable names, numbers (in decimal, binary, or hex), and operators for integer expressions. Comments begin with a semicolon and run to end of line.

Syntactic level: instructions that follow UDVM opcodes (like LOAD, COPY, INPUT-BITS), directives for padding and memory layout (like pad, align, at), and labels to mark memory addresses. Instructions can take operands that reference memory locations (prefixed with $) or literal values.
sections.plainLanguage: The assembly language is like a recipe written in a simple dialect. You tell the machine what to copy, what to move around, and where to jump to next.

sections.title: Compression Algorithms
sections.content:
The RFC covers five compression algorithms, each trading off compression ratio, memory use, processing time, and code complexity:

LZ77: References previously decompressed text by position and length. Simple but produces large compressed messages unless many repeated strings exist.

LZSS: Improves on LZ77 by prefixing each token with a 1-bit flag indicating whether the next item is a literal byte or a position/length pair.

LZW: Maintains a codebook of frequently seen text strings. Each compressed token references a codebook entry, allowing adaptive compression as the decompressor learns the message structure.

DEFLATE: The algorithm used in gzip, employing Huffman codes and position/length pairs. The RFC covers only fixed Huffman codes (block type 01) for simplicity.

LZJH: The ITU-T Recommendation V.44 algorithm. Maintains an adaptive codebook with string extension support, offering the highest compression but also the most complex implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: Five different squeezing methods: LZ77 copies old stuff, LZSS marks literals with flags, LZW learns common patterns, DEFLATE uses Huffman codes, and LZJH combines several tricks.

sections.title: Robustness Mechanisms
sections.content:
In lossy networks, packets can be lost or arrive out of order. SigComp offers mechanisms to detect and recover from corruption:

Acknowledgements: The SigComp feedback mechanism can carry a state identifier back to the sender. The sender should not access saved state until acknowledging reception, ensuring the receiver has the bytecode.

Static Dictionaries: Common protocol-specific text strings (like SIP or SDP headers) can be pre-loaded as a static state item, improving compression without re-uploading the dictionary.

CRC Checksum: A cyclic redundancy check over the decompressed message detects corruption that decompression might not catch.

Resource Announcements: Endpoints can advertise their available processing, memory, and state identifiers via the feedback mechanism, allowing the remote end to optimize compression choices.
sections.plainLanguage: Robustness features: ask the receiver to confirm they got the bytecode, use pre-made pattern libraries, check if squeezing worked without errors, and tell the sender how much power you have.

sections.title: Choosing an Algorithm
sections.content:
Implementers should consider five factors when selecting a compression algorithm:

  • Compression ratio: LZJH typically achieves the best ratio, DEFLATE is competitive, LZW and LZSS are good, and LZ77 is simplest.
  • Memory requirements: All examples assume 16K decompression memory, 8K state memory, and 16 cycles per bit. Smaller memory devices may not support LZJH or DEFLATE.
  • Processing time: LZ77 is fast; LZJH requires more computation.
  • Bytecode size: Smaller bytecode means faster initial state upload. LZ77 is smallest; LZJH is largest.
  • Intellectual Property: Some algorithms are covered by patents. DEFLATE is widely licensed; LZW has patent concerns in some jurisdictions.

Most protocols will benefit from using either DEFLATE for good balance or LZJH if compression ratio is paramount and resources permit.
sections.plainLanguage: Ask yourself: how small do messages need to be, how much memory do I have, is speed important, and are there patent issues? The answers guide your choice.
